cic_karr_1989.title: Clarence Karr, “What Happened to Canadian Intellectual History?” Acadiensis 18, no. 2 (Spring 1989): 158–74 (review essay).
cic_karr_1989.citation: Clarence Karr, “What Happened to Canadian Intellectual History?” Acadiensis 18, no. 2 (Spring 1989): 158–74 (review essay).

verification.note: Full text read (answers/research/q11-intellectual-history-critique.json). Analyses the field's 'preoccupation with delineating the national mind', its 'propensity to place everything in an atmosphere of crisis' and 'its narrow, elitist, biographical methodology' (p. 160); group biography after Berger's Sense of Power focuses on 'an elite group composed primarily of academics, journalists and clergymen' (p. 169), leaving little known of what the population thought. Names Berger, McKillop, Cook, Shortt, Levitt, Allen and Francis; calls the books 'excellent studies within their self-imposed context'. Checked against: Acadiensis article page and full text (https://journals.lib.unb.ca/index.php/Acadiensis/article/view/12284; https://journals.lib.unb.ca/index.php/Acadiensis/article/download/12284/13128); Érudit record (https://www.erudit.org/en/journals/acadiensis/1989-v18-n2-acadiensis_18_2/acad18_2re04/). Addendum 2026-10-14: Re-read 2026-10-14 for the Berger person entry (Acadiensis PDF, pp. 158–174, page numbers from running heads). p. 160: 'Ever since Carl Berger used this basic approach in his impressive study of imperialism in the early 1970s, many have adopted his methodology'; p. 161: Berger 'rescued the previously outcast imperialists and transformed them into significant Canadian nationalists' and 'As a sequel he analysed the national conceptual frameworks in which professional historians functioned and wrote'; pp. 162–163: 'over-Canadianization of imperialism' and Carr's 'scavenger hunt for nationalism' (n. 20: Carr 1982; Cole 1970, 1971; Page 1970); p. 167: group biography 'upheld by many historians in Canada as the best method'; p. 168: Berger's premise (Sense of Power, p. 12, per n. 36) and 'whatever a single advocate chooses to believe'. [cook draft: Re-read for the 1.135 Ramsay Cook entry (UNB PDF, pp. 161–163). Quoted: Levitt and Cook 'deepened our understanding of Henri Bourassa' (p. 161, n. 11 citing Canada and the French-Canadian Question under a slipped title); 'it was Ramsay Cook who did so much to heighten English Canada's understanding of French-Canadian nationalism who led the anti-national crusade'; Cook's 1970 'Sisyphus' passage (n. 17: Saturday Night, April 1970, p. 19, and the South Atlantic Quarterly essay); The Regenerators' subjects 'almost never alluded to the cultivation of a national sentiment' (n. 18, Regenerators p. 6); 'problems inherent in extremes on both sides'; n. 18, 'while Cook is opposed to divisive nationalism, he is a centralist' (p. 162); n. 21, 'an equally forceful Ontario bias' (p. 163).]

cic_karr_1989.scope_note: Critique: national mind, crisis framing, and an elitist group-biography method.

pe135_berger_mills_1977.title: Allen Mills, review of Carl Berger, The Writing of Canadian History: Aspects of English-Canadian Historical Writing, 1900–1970 (Toronto: Oxford University Press, 1976), Canadian Journal of Political and Social Theory 1, no. 1 (1977): 134–137.
pe135_berger_mills_1977.citation: Allen Mills, review of Carl Berger, The Writing of Canadian History (1976), Canadian Journal of Political and Social Theory / Revue canadienne de théorie politique et sociale 1, no. 1 (1977): 134–137.

verification.note: Read in full (journal PDF on the UVic OJS archive; issue table of contents gives Allen Mills, pp. 134–137; issue published 30 April 1977). Quoted: The Sense of Power saw the imperialists' ideas 'as essentially a species of Canadian nationalism'; the new book 'makes a substantial contribution to the intellectual history of English Canada'; the 'superluminaries' and 'the book is really about them' (p. 135); Berger's 'main criticism of English-Canadian historians' (pp. 135–136) with Berger's 1976 pp. 259–260 quoted; 'places much too much weight on that over-used term' and 'very different conceptions of the nation that is to survive' (p. 136); the claim about class, region, culture and family 'is unimpeachable' (pp. 136–137); the last chapter 'all too brief' (p. 137).

pe135_berger_mills_1977.scope_note: In-period review: the book as intellectual history; nationalism as Berger's charge against the tradition, and its limits.

pe135_berger_monet_1972.title: Jacques Monet, review of Carl Berger, The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867–1914 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1970), Revue d'histoire de l'Amérique française 26, no. 2 (September 1972): 274–276.
pe135_berger_monet_1972.citation: Jacques Monet, s.j., compte rendu de Carl Berger, The Sense of Power (1970), Revue d'histoire de l'Amérique française 26, no. 2 (1972): 274–276. doi:10.7202/303178ar.

verification.note: Read in full (Érudit PDF, text layer; header gives 'University of Toronto Press, 1970. 277 p.'). Quoted: imperialists 'ont eu très mauvaise presse parmi les historiens du Canada'; English-Canadian historians 'partisans pour la plupart de l'explication de l'équipe gagnante' saw them as 'des conservateurs retardataires'; Berger 'vient maintenant nuancer ces jugements... téméraires' (p. 274); the imperialists were not 'des agents d'une puissance étrangère' but 'de vrais Canadians nationalistes' (pp. 274–275); the thesis, 'déjà suggérée par la monographie de Norman Penlington', 'sera dorénavant très difficile, sinon impossible, à réfuter'; earlier criticisms: economic and military neglect, pan-Britannic witnesses, 'une petite élite' (p. 275; notes cite R. J. D. Page, JCS Aug. 1970, 39–43; D. L. Cole, JCS, 44–49; H. V. Nelles, Canadian Forum April–May 1970, 10–12; the OCR misplaces the note numbers but keeps their order); 'une contribution majeure — sinon un premier modèle — à l'histoire des idées (oui, il y en a) au Canada anglophone' and French Canadians' 'toute petite' place in imperialist thought (p. 276). Cites the book at pp. 132 and 261, which confirms that the 2013 reprint keeps the 1970 pagination.

pe135_berger_monet_1972.scope_note: In-period francophone review: the imperialism thesis, its novelty, its first critics.

w1_daston_moral_economy_1995.title: Lorraine Daston, “The Moral Economy of Science,” Osiris 10 (1995): 3–24.
w1_daston_moral_economy_1995.citation: Lorraine Daston, “The Moral Economy of Science,” Osiris 10 (1995): 3–24.

verification.note: Read in part (pp. 3–4) for revision 1.144 in the Max Planck Society PuRe public PDF (item_2276978). p. 3: "I will nonetheless claim that not only does science have what I will call a moral economy (indeed, several); these moral economies are moreover constitutive of those features conventionally (and, to my mind, correctly) deemed most characteristic of science as a way of knowing … certain forms of empiricism, quantification, and objectivity itself are not simply compatible with moral economies; they require moral economies." p. 3 n. 1: "my use of the term moral economy diverges significantly from E. P. Thompson's in 'The Moral Economy of the English Crowd in the Eighteenth Century' … My appeal here to 'economies' of affects and values has little to do with Thompson's accounts of corn markets … although it does appeal to a broader sense of 'legitimizing notion.'" n. 2 gathers Hannaway, Porter, Schaffer and Shapin. p. 4: "a web of affect-saturated values that stand and function in well-defined relationship to one another"; "As Gaston Bachelard decades ago remarked, to imbue objects or actions with emotion is almost always thereby to valorize them". pp. 5–24 unread. The second research pass (evidence-daston.pass2.md §1) read pp. 3–5 and 21–24 in another scan (www.ias.edu/sites/default/files/sss/pdfs/Moral-Daston.pdf): p. 5, "To extend Ludwik Fleck's terminology, what is meant here is a Gefühls- as well as a Denkkollektiv", n. 7 and p. 22 on Elias's "civilizing process", pp. 21–22 on mechanical and "aperspectival objectivity", and pp. 23–24: moral economies "are part of what one might call historical epistemology—a history of the categories of facticity, evidence, objectivity, and so forth". That pass cites the article as pp. 2–24; the article's first page prints "OSIRIS 1995, 10: 3-24" and p. 2 is the frontispiece, so 3–24 is kept.
